items.stem: What is the momentum of a 1500 kg car moving at 20 m s⁻¹?
items.answer: 30 000 kg m s⁻¹

items.stem: Explain how a car crumple zone reduces the force on passengers in a collision.
items.answer: The passengers' change in momentum is fixed; the crumple zone increases the time over which the momentum changes, so the rate of change of momentum, and hence the force, is smaller.
items.markingKey: Δp fixed [1]; longer time [1]; F = Δp/Δt smaller [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why a cricketer moves the hands backwards when catching a fast ball.
items.answer: This increases the time taken to stop the ball for the same change in momentum, reducing the force on the hands.
items.markingKey: increases stopping time [1]; F = Δp/Δt reduced [1] [2]

items.stem: A golf ball of mass 0.046 kg moving at 25 m s⁻¹ hits a wall and rebounds along the same line at 12 m s⁻¹. It is in contact with the wall for 10 ms. Work out the average force exerted by the wall on the ball.
items.markingKey: F = Δp/Δt = 0.046 × (25 + 12)/0.010 = 170 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A squash ball of mass 0.024 kg moving at 25 m s⁻¹ hits a wall and rebounds along the same line at 8.0 m s⁻¹. It is in contact with the wall for 20 ms. Calculate the change in momentum and the average force on the ball.
items.answer: Δp = 0.792 kg m s⁻¹ away from the wall; F = 39.6 N
items.markingKey: Δp = m(v − u) with sign convention = 0.792 kg m s⁻¹ [1]; F = Δp/Δt [1]; = 39.6 N [1] [3]

items.stem: A squash ball of mass 0.024 kg moving at 25 m s⁻¹ hits a wall and rebounds along the same line at 12 m s⁻¹. It is in contact with the wall for 20 ms. (a) Calculate the average force on the ball. (b) State the force exerted by the ball on the wall and the law used. (c) Explain why a softer ball with the same speeds would exert a smaller force.
items.answer: (a) 44.4 N (b) 44.4 N towards the wall, by Newton's third law (c) longer contact time, so smaller rate of change of momentum.
items.markingKey: (a) Δp = 0.888 kg m s⁻¹ [1]; F = 44.4 N [1] (b) equal and opposite, N3 [1] (c) Δt larger, F = Δp/Δt smaller [1] [4]

items.stem: A 60 kg stunt performer falling at 8.0 m s⁻¹ lands either on hard ground (stopping time 0.12 s) or on an air cushion (stopping time 1.0 s). (a) Explain why the longer stopping time is safer. (b) State Newton's second law in terms of momentum. (c) Calculate the average deceleration in the shorter collision.
items.answer: (a) The same Δp over a longer time gives a smaller force (and deceleration), so less injury. (b) The resultant force is proportional to (equal to) the rate of change of momentum. (c) 66.7 m s⁻²
items.markingKey: (a) same Δp, longer t [1]; smaller force [1] [2] (b) The resultant force is proportional to (equal to) the rate of change of momentum [1] (c) a = v/t: 66.7 m s⁻² [1]

items.stem: A 70 kg stunt performer falling at 8.0 m s⁻¹ lands either on hard ground (stopping time 0.12 s) or on an air cushion (stopping time 0.60 s). (a) Calculate the change in momentum. (b) Explain why the longer stopping time is safer. (c) State Newton's second law in terms of momentum. (d) Calculate the average deceleration in the shorter collision.
items.answer: (a) 560 kg m s⁻¹ (b) The same Δp over a longer time gives a smaller force (and deceleration), so less injury. (c) The resultant force is proportional to (equal to) the rate of change of momentum. (d) 66.7 m s⁻²
items.markingKey: (a) Δp = mv: 560 kg m s⁻¹ [1] (b) same Δp, longer t [1]; smaller force [1] [2] (c) The resultant force is proportional to (equal to) the rate of change of momentum [1] (d) a = v/t: 66.7 m s⁻² [1]

items.stem: Which unit is equivalent to kg m s⁻¹?
items.answer: N s
items.markingKey: Impulse FΔt = Δp, so N s = kg m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Which statement is Newton's second law in terms of momentum?
options: The momentum is equal to force × distance
The resultant force is equal to the rate of change of momentum
The momentum of a system is always zero
The resultant force is equal to the change of momentum
items.answer: The resultant force is equal to the rate of change of momentum
items.markingKey: F = Δp/Δt.

items.stem: A ball of mass 0.20 kg hits a wall at 5.0 m s⁻¹ and rebounds at 5.0 m s⁻¹. What is the magnitude of its change in momentum?
items.answer: 2.0 kg m s⁻¹

items.stem: Explain why a ball that bounces back from a wall experiences a larger force than one that stops dead in the same time.
items.answer: Momentum is a vector; rebounding reverses the velocity, so the change in momentum is larger (up to double), and so the force (Δp/Δt) is larger.
items.markingKey: Δp larger when direction reverses [1]; F = Δp/Δt [1] [2]

items.stem: Show that F = ma is a special case of F = Δp/Δt.
items.answer: Δp/Δt = Δ(mv)/Δt; for constant mass, = m Δv/Δt = ma.
items.markingKey: mass constant taken out [1]; Δv/Δt = a [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why momentum is a vector quantity.
items.answer: p = mv; mass is a scalar and velocity is a vector, so their product has direction (the direction of the velocity).
items.markingKey: velocity is a vector [1]; momentum in direction of velocity [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why a cricketer moves the hands backwards when catching a fast ball. (b) Explain how a car crumple zone reduces the force on passengers in a collision.
items.answer: (a) This increases the time taken to stop the ball for the same change in momentum, reducing the force on the hands. (b) The passengers' change in momentum is fixed; the crumple zone increases the time over which the momentum changes, so the rate of change of momentum, and hence the force, is smaller.
items.markingKey: (a) increases stopping time [1]; F = Δp/Δt reduced [1] [2] (b) Δp fixed [1]; longer time [1]; F = Δp/Δt smaller [1] [3]

items.stem: A garden sprinkler jet strikes a vertical board horizontally and the water falls away. Water leaves the hose at 15 m s⁻¹ at a rate of 3.0 kg s⁻¹. Calculate the force exerted on the wall by the water.
items.markingKey: momentum lost per second = (mass per second) × v [1]; F = 3.0 × 15 [1]; = 45 N [1] [3]

items.stem: The force on a ball of mass 0.40 kg, initially at rest, during a kick rises uniformly from zero to 600 N and then falls uniformly to zero, the whole contact lasting 40 ms. Calculate the speed of the ball after the kick.
items.answer: 30 m s⁻¹
items.markingKey: impulse = area of triangle = ½ × 600 × 0.040 = 12 N s [1]; = Δp [1]; v = 12/0.40 = 30 m s⁻¹ [1] [3]

items.stem: A football of mass 0.43 kg moving at 15 m s⁻¹ hits a wall and rebounds along the same line at 8.0 m s⁻¹. It is in contact with the wall for 10 ms. Work out the average force exerted by the wall on the ball.
items.markingKey: F = Δp/Δt = 0.43 × (15 + 8.0)/0.010 = 989 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A fire hose sends a horizontal jet of water against a door; the water does not bounce back. Water leaves the hose at 10 m s⁻¹ at a rate of 3.0 kg s⁻¹. Calculate the force exerted on the wall by the water.
items.markingKey: momentum lost per second = (mass per second) × v [1]; F = 3.0 × 10 [1]; = 30 N [1] [3]

items.stem: A tennis ball of mass 0.057 kg moving at 10 m s⁻¹ hits a wall and stops. It is in contact with the wall for 10 ms. (a) Calculate the average force on the ball. (b) State the force exerted by the ball on the wall and the law used. (c) Explain why a softer ball with the same speeds would exert a smaller force.
items.answer: (a) 57.0 N (b) 57.0 N towards the wall, by Newton's third law (c) longer contact time, so smaller rate of change of momentum.

items.stem: A 75 kg stunt performer falling at 12 m s⁻¹ lands either on hard ground (stopping time 0.080 s) or on an air cushion (stopping time 0.80 s). (a) Explain why the longer stopping time is safer. (b) Calculate the average deceleration in the shorter collision.
items.answer: (a) The same Δp over a longer time gives a smaller force (and deceleration), so less injury. (b) 150 m s⁻²

items.stem: A 75 kg stunt performer falling at 10 m s⁻¹ lands either on hard ground (stopping time 0.12 s) or on an air cushion (stopping time 1.0 s). (a) Calculate the change in momentum. (b) Explain why the longer stopping time is safer. (c) State Newton's second law in terms of momentum.
items.answer: (a) 750 kg m s⁻¹ (b) The same Δp over a longer time gives a smaller force (and deceleration), so less injury. (c) The resultant force is proportional to (equal to) the rate of change of momentum.

items.stem: State the principle of conservation of momentum.
items.answer: The total momentum of a system of interacting objects remains constant provided no resultant external force acts.
items.markingKey: total momentum constant [1]; no external resultant force [1] [2]

items.stem: Use Newton's third law to explain why momentum is conserved when two trolleys collide.
items.answer: During the collision each trolley exerts an equal and opposite force on the other for the same time; so their momentum changes are equal and opposite and the total momentum is unchanged.
items.markingKey: equal and opposite forces (N3) [1]; same contact time [1]; equal and opposite Δp [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why a rifle recoils when it fires a bullet.
items.answer: Total momentum is zero before firing; the bullet gains forward momentum so the rifle must gain equal backward momentum.
items.markingKey: initial momentum zero [1]; rifle gains equal and opposite momentum [1] [2]

items.stem: Trolley A of mass 0.50 kg moving at 4.0 m s⁻¹ collides with trolley B of mass 1.5 kg, which is at rest. They stick together. Work out the speed immediately after the collision.
items.answer: 1.0 m s⁻¹
items.markingKey: v = (m₁u₁ + m₂u₂)/(m₁ + m₂) = (2.0 + 0)/2.0 = 1.0 m s⁻¹. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Car A of mass 1200 kg moving at 12 m s⁻¹ collides with car B of mass 1000 kg, which moves at 5.0 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction. They stick together. Calculate the common velocity after the collision, stating its direction.
items.answer: 4.27 m s⁻¹ in the original direction of car A
items.markingKey: momentum before = 9400 kg m s⁻¹ (signs) [1]; ÷ total mass [1]; 4.27 m s⁻¹ with direction [1] [3]

items.stem: Car A of mass 1200 kg moving at 15 m s⁻¹ collides with car B of mass 1000 kg, which is at rest. They stick together. (a) Calculate their common velocity. (b) Calculate the loss of kinetic energy. (c) State what happens to this energy.
items.answer: (a) 8.18 m s⁻¹ (b) 61 400 J (c) transferred to thermal energy, sound and deformation of the bodies.
items.markingKey: (a) conservation of momentum [1]; v = 8.18 m s⁻¹ [1] (b) KE before 1.35 × 10⁵ J, after 73 600 J [1]; loss 61 400 J [1] (c) heat/sound/deformation [1] [5]

items.stem: In a forensic test in Colombo, a 0.015 kg pellet moving at 250 m s⁻¹ is fired into a suspended 1.5 kg block, which swings upwards. (a) Calculate the height to which the block rises. (b) State and explain whether the collision is elastic.
items.answer: (a) 0.312 m (b) Inelastic: kinetic energy is not conserved (most becomes thermal energy and deformation).
items.markingKey: (a) h = V²/(2g) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 0.312 m with unit [1] [2] (b) inelastic [1]; KE lost [1] [2]

items.stem: A bullet of mass 0.015 kg travelling horizontally at 300 m s⁻¹ embeds itself in a wooden block of mass 1.0 kg hanging at rest from strings (a ballistic pendulum). (a) Calculate the percentage of the bullet's kinetic energy that is lost in the impact. (b) Explain why momentum is conserved during the impact even though the strings exert forces.
items.answer: (a) 98.5% (b) The impact is very brief and the strings are vertical, so there is no horizontal external force during the impact.
items.markingKey: (a) KE after/KE before = m/(m + M) (equation) [1]; substitution [1]; answer 98.5% with unit [1] [3] (b) no horizontal external force [1]; short duration [1] [2]

items.stem: A 2.0 kg trolley moving at 3.0 m s⁻¹ collides with and sticks to a stationary 1.0 kg trolley. What is their common velocity?
items.answer: 2.0 m s⁻¹

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) State the principle of conservation of momentum. (b) Two skaters at rest push apart. The 60 kg skater moves at 2.0 m s⁻¹. How fast does the 40 kg skater move?
items.answer: (a) The total momentum of a system of interacting objects remains constant provided no resultant external force acts. (b) 3.0 m s⁻¹
items.markingKey: (a) total momentum constant [1]; no external resultant force [1] [2] (b) 60 × 2.0 = 40v → v = 3.0 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Explain why the momentum of a ball falling towards the Earth is not conserved, but the momentum of the ball and the Earth together is.
items.answer: Weight is an external force on the ball alone, so its momentum changes; for ball + Earth the gravitational forces are internal and equal and opposite, so total momentum is constant.
items.markingKey: external force on ball alone [1]; internal forces for the system [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe how momentum is conserved when a stationary nucleus emits an α-particle.
items.answer: Total momentum is zero before; afterwards the α-particle and the daughter nucleus move in opposite directions with equal magnitudes of momentum.
items.markingKey: zero total before [1]; equal and opposite momenta after [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why the momentum of a ball falling towards the Earth is not conserved, but the momentum of the ball and the Earth together is. (b) Describe how momentum is conserved when a stationary nucleus emits an α-particle.
items.answer: (a) Weight is an external force on the ball alone, so its momentum changes; for ball + Earth the gravitational forces are internal and equal and opposite, so total momentum is constant. (b) Total momentum is zero before; afterwards the α-particle and the daughter nucleus move in opposite directions with equal magnitudes of momentum.
items.markingKey: (a) external force on ball alone [1]; internal forces for the system [1] [2] (b) zero total before [1]; equal and opposite momenta after [1] [2]

items.stem: Car A of mass 1200 kg moving at 15 m s⁻¹ collides with car B of mass 1000 kg, which moves at 5.0 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction. They stick together. Calculate the speed immediately after the collision.

items.stem: A stationary firework of mass 3.0 kg explodes into two pieces. A piece of mass 0.75 kg moves off at 12 m s⁻¹. Calculate the velocity of the other piece.
items.answer: 4.0 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction
items.markingKey: total momentum zero [1]; 0.75 × 12 = 2.25 × v [1]; v = 4.0 m s⁻¹ opposite [1] [3]

items.stem: A stationary firework of mass 2.0 kg explodes into two pieces. A piece of mass 0.50 kg moves off at 10 m s⁻¹. Calculate the velocity of the other piece.
items.answer: 3.33 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction
items.markingKey: total momentum zero [1]; 0.50 × 10 = 1.5 × v [1]; v = 3.33 m s⁻¹ opposite [1] [3]

items.stem: In a perfectly elastic collision, which quantities are conserved?
options: Both total momentum and total kinetic energy
items.answer: Both total momentum and total kinetic energy
items.markingKey: Elastic: KE conserved; momentum is always conserved in an isolated system.

items.stem: Explain why total energy is always conserved in a collision even though kinetic energy may not be.
items.answer: Energy cannot be created or destroyed; kinetic energy lost is transferred to other stores such as thermal energy, sound and deformation (strain) energy.
items.markingKey: total energy conserved [1]; KE transferred to other forms [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how to test whether a collision between two gliders on an air track is elastic using only velocity measurements.
items.answer: Measure the velocities before and after; calculate the relative speed of approach and of separation; if they are equal the collision is perfectly elastic.
items.markingKey: measure velocities [1]; compare relative speeds of approach and separation [1] [2]

items.stem: A glider of mass 2.0 kg moving at 2.0 m s⁻¹ on an air track hits a stationary glider of mass 0.50 kg. Afterwards, the second glider moves at 2.24 m s⁻¹. Calculate the speed of the first glider after the collision.
items.markingKey: 2.0 × 2.0 = 2.0v₁ + 0.50 × 2.24 = 1.44 m s⁻¹. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A glider of mass 1.0 kg moving at 4.0 m s⁻¹ on an air track hits a stationary glider of mass 1.0 kg. Afterwards, the second glider moves at 4.0 m s⁻¹. Calculate the velocity of the first glider after the collision and determine whether the collision is elastic using relative speeds.
items.answer: v₁ = 0 m s⁻¹; approach 4.0 m s⁻¹, separation 4.0 m s⁻¹, so the collision is elastic.
items.markingKey: momentum: v₁ = 0 m s⁻¹ [1]; relative speed of approach = 4.0 m s⁻¹ [1]; separation = 4.0 − (0) = 4.0 m s⁻¹ [1]; conclusion [1] [4]

items.stem: In a physics laboratory in Toronto, a glider of mass 3.0 kg moving at 6.0 m s⁻¹ collides with a stationary glider of mass 2.0 kg on a level air track. (a) The gliders stick together. Calculate their common speed. (b) For the sticking collision, calculate the kinetic energy lost.
items.markingKey: (a) conservation of momentum (method/substitution) [1]; answer 3.6 m s⁻¹ with unit [1] [2] (b) KE before − KE after (method/substitution) [1]; answer 21.6 J with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: For a perfectly elastic collision between two bodies, the relative speed of approach is …
options: equal to the relative speed of separation
less than the relative speed of separation
greater than the relative speed of separation
items.answer: equal to the relative speed of separation
items.markingKey: This follows from conservation of both momentum and KE.

items.stem: A ball dropped onto a hard floor rebounds to almost the same height. Explain what this shows about the collision.
items.answer: The rebound speed nearly equals the impact speed, so very little kinetic energy is lost: the collision is nearly elastic.
items.markingKey: speeds nearly equal [1]; KE nearly conserved/nearly elastic [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why, in a head-on elastic collision between equal masses with one initially at rest, the moving body stops.
items.answer: Momentum and KE conservation together require the velocities to be exchanged: the first stops and the second moves off with the original velocity.
items.markingKey: both conservation laws applied [1]; velocities exchanged [1] [2]

items.stem: Two identical trolleys, each of mass 0.50 kg, collide head-on, each moving at 5.0 m s⁻¹, and stop dead. Grace says "momentum was lost, so this breaks the law of conservation of momentum." Explain why Grace is wrong, and state what happened to the kinetic energy.
items.answer: The total momentum before was zero (equal and opposite momenta), and it is zero after, so momentum is conserved. All 12.5 J of kinetic energy was transferred to thermal energy, sound and deformation (a totally inelastic collision).
items.markingKey: momenta equal and opposite: total zero before [1]; zero after so conserved [1]; KE transferred to other forms [1] [3]

items.stem: Two identical trolleys, each of mass 0.50 kg, collide head-on, each moving at 4.0 m s⁻¹, and stop dead. Daniel says "momentum was lost, so this breaks the law of conservation of momentum." Explain why Daniel is wrong, and state what happened to the kinetic energy.
items.answer: The total momentum before was zero (equal and opposite momenta), and it is zero after, so momentum is conserved. All 8.0 J of kinetic energy was transferred to thermal energy, sound and deformation (a totally inelastic collision).
items.markingKey: momenta equal and opposite: total zero before [1]; zero after so conserved [1]; KE transferred to other forms [1] [3]

items.stem: Sphere A of mass 2.0 kg moving at 4.0 m s⁻¹ has a perfectly elastic head-on collision with sphere B of mass 4.0 kg, which moves at 1.0 m s⁻¹ in the same direction. Using conservation of momentum and the relative speed of approach equals the relative speed of separation, determine the velocities of A and B after the collision.
items.answer: A: 0 m s⁻¹, B: 3.0 m s⁻¹ (positive = original direction of A)

items.stem: Sphere A of mass 1.0 kg moving at 4.0 m s⁻¹ has a perfectly elastic head-on collision with sphere B of mass 2.0 kg, which moves at 2.0 m s⁻¹ towards it. Using conservation of momentum and the relative speed of approach equals the relative speed of separation, determine the velocities of A and B after the collision.
items.answer: A: −4.0 m s⁻¹, B: 2.0 m s⁻¹ (positive = original direction of A)

items.stem: A glider of mass 1.0 kg moving at 2.0 m s⁻¹ on an air track hits a stationary glider of mass 0.50 kg. Afterwards, the second glider moves at 2.13 m s⁻¹. Calculate the velocity of the first glider after the collision and determine whether the collision is elastic using relative speeds.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why momentum is a vector quantity. (b) Explain why a ball that bounces back from a wall experiences a larger force than one that stops dead in the same time.
items.answer: (a) p = mv; mass is a scalar and velocity is a vector, so their product has direction (the direction of the velocity). (b) Momentum is a vector; rebounding reverses the velocity, so the change in momentum is larger (up to double), and so the force (Δp/Δt) is larger.
items.markingKey: (a) velocity is a vector [1]; momentum in direction of velocity [1] [2] (b) Δp larger when direction reverses [1]; F = Δp/Δt [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain how a car crumple zone reduces the force on passengers in a collision. (b) Explain why a ball that bounces back from a wall experiences a larger force than one that stops dead in the same time.
items.answer: (a) The passengers' change in momentum is fixed; the crumple zone increases the time over which the momentum changes, so the rate of change of momentum, and hence the force, is smaller. (b) Momentum is a vector; rebounding reverses the velocity, so the change in momentum is larger (up to double), and so the force (Δp/Δt) is larger.
items.markingKey: (a) Δp fixed [1]; longer time [1]; F = Δp/Δt smaller [1] [3] (b) Δp larger when direction reverses [1]; F = Δp/Δt [1] [2]

items.stem: A fire hose sends a horizontal jet of water against a door; the water does not bounce back. Water leaves the hose at 15 m s⁻¹ at a rate of 4.0 kg s⁻¹. Calculate the force exerted on the wall by the water.
items.markingKey: momentum lost per second = (mass per second) × v [1]; F = 4.0 × 15 [1]; = 60 N [1] [3]

items.stem: A squash ball of mass 0.024 kg moving at 10 m s⁻¹ hits a wall and rebounds along the same line at 12 m s⁻¹. It is in contact with the wall for 8.0 ms. Calculate the average force exerted by the wall on the ball.
items.markingKey: F = Δp/Δt = 0.024 × (10 + 12)/0.0080 = 66 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: The force on a ball of mass 0.15 kg, initially at rest, during a kick rises uniformly from zero to 200 N and then falls uniformly to zero, the whole contact lasting 40 ms. Calculate the speed of the ball after the kick.

A 60 kg stunt performer falling at 12 m s⁻¹ lands either on hard ground (stopping time 0.10 s) or on an air cushion (stopping time 0.60 s). (a) Calculate the change in momentum. (b) Explain why the longer stopping time is safer. (c) Calculate the average deceleration in the shorter collision.
items.answer: (a) 720 kg m s⁻¹ (b) The same Δp over a longer time gives a smaller force (and deceleration), so less injury. (c) 120 m s⁻²
items.markingKey: (a) Δp = mv: 720 kg m s⁻¹ [1] (b) same Δp, longer t [1]; smaller force [1] [2] (c) a = v/t: 120 m s⁻² [1]

items.stem: In a crash test in Cape Town, a dummy of mass 60 kg travelling at 12 m s⁻¹ is brought to rest. Without an airbag the stopping time is 0.12 s; with an airbag it is 0.60 s. (a) Calculate the change in momentum. (b) Calculate the average force in each case. (c) Explain why the longer stopping time is safer. (d) State Newton's second law in terms of momentum.
items.answer: (a) 720 kg m s⁻¹ (b) 6000 N and 1200 N (c) The same Δp over a longer time gives a smaller force (and deceleration), so less injury. (d) The resultant force is proportional to (equal to) the rate of change of momentum.
items.markingKey: (a) Δp = mv: 720 kg m s⁻¹ [1] (b) F = Δp/Δt for each (method/substitution) [1]; answer 6000 N and 1200 N with unit [1] [2] (c) same Δp, longer t [1]; smaller force [1] [2] (d) The resultant force is proportional to (equal to) the rate of change of momentum [1]

items.stem: A gun recoils when it fires a bullet. Before firing, the total momentum is zero. After firing, the total momentum is …
options: twice the momentum of the bullet
equal to the kinetic energy of the bullet
equal to the momentum of the bullet
items.answer: zero
items.markingKey: No external horizontal force: momentum conserved; bullet and gun have equal and opposite momenta.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Describe how momentum is conserved when a stationary nucleus emits an α-particle. (b) Use Newton's third law to explain why momentum is conserved when two trolleys collide.
items.answer: (a) Total momentum is zero before; afterwards the α-particle and the daughter nucleus move in opposite directions with equal magnitudes of momentum. (b) During the collision each trolley exerts an equal and opposite force on the other for the same time; so their momentum changes are equal and opposite and the total momentum is unchanged.
items.markingKey: (a) zero total before [1]; equal and opposite momenta after [1] [2] (b) equal and opposite forces (N3) [1]; same contact time [1]; equal and opposite Δp [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why the momentum of a ball falling towards the Earth is not conserved, but the momentum of the ball and the Earth together is. (b) Use Newton's third law to explain why momentum is conserved when two trolleys collide.
items.answer: (a) Weight is an external force on the ball alone, so its momentum changes; for ball + Earth the gravitational forces are internal and equal and opposite, so total momentum is constant. (b) During the collision each trolley exerts an equal and opposite force on the other for the same time; so their momentum changes are equal and opposite and the total momentum is unchanged.
items.markingKey: (a) external force on ball alone [1]; internal forces for the system [1] [2] (b) equal and opposite forces (N3) [1]; same contact time [1]; equal and opposite Δp [1] [3]

items.stem: Trolley A of mass 0.80 kg moving at 2.0 m s⁻¹ collides with trolley B of mass 2.5 kg, which is at rest. They stick together. Calculate the speed immediately after the collision.

items.stem: Two trolleys of total mass 6.0 kg are held together at rest with a compressed spring between them. When released, the 1.5 kg trolley moves at 10 m s⁻¹. Calculate the velocity of the other piece.

items.stem: A puck on an air table of mass 2.0 kg moving at 5.0 m s⁻¹ strikes an identical stationary one. items.stem: In a forensic test in Manila, a 0.015 kg pellet moving at 250 m s⁻¹ is fired into a suspended 1.5 kg block, which swings upwards. (a) Calculate the percentage of the bullet's kinetic energy that is lost in the impact. (b) State and explain whether the collision is elastic.
items.answer: (a) 99.0% (b) Inelastic: kinetic energy is not conserved (most becomes thermal energy and deformation).
items.markingKey: (a) KE after/KE before = m/(m + M) (equation) [1]; substitution [1]; answer 99.0% with unit [1] [3] (b) inelastic [1]; KE lost [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Two balls approach each other at 3.0 m s⁻¹ and 2.0 m s⁻¹. What is their relative speed of approach? (b) In a perfectly elastic collision, which quantities are conserved?
items.answer: (a) 5.0 m s⁻¹ (b) Both total momentum and total kinetic energy
items.markingKey: (a) Opposite directions: relative speed = 3.0 + 2.0. (b) Elastic: KE conserved; momentum is always conserved in an isolated system.

items.stem: Two identical trolleys, each of mass 0.50 kg, collide head-on, each moving at 5.0 m s⁻¹, and stop dead. Kenji says "momentum was lost, so this breaks the law of conservation of momentum." Explain why Kenji is wrong, and state what happened to the kinetic energy.
items.answer: The total momentum before was zero (equal and opposite momenta), and it is zero after, so momentum is conserved. All 12.5 J of kinetic energy was transferred to thermal energy, sound and deformation (a totally inelastic collision).
items.markingKey: momenta equal and opposite: total zero before [1]; zero after so conserved [1]; KE transferred to other forms [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why total energy is always conserved in a collision even though kinetic energy may not be. (b) Explain how to test whether a collision between two gliders on an air track is elastic using only velocity measurements.
items.answer: (a) Energy cannot be created or destroyed; kinetic energy lost is transferred to other stores such as thermal energy, sound and deformation (strain) energy. (b) Measure the velocities before and after; calculate the relative speed of approach and of separation; if they are equal the collision is perfectly elastic.
items.markingKey: (a) total energy conserved [1]; KE transferred to other forms [1] [2] (b) measure velocities [1]; compare relative speeds of approach and separation [1] [2]

items.stem: A glider of mass 2.0 kg moving at 6.0 m s⁻¹ on an air track hits a stationary glider of mass 1.5 kg. Afterwards, the second glider moves at 4.8 m s⁻¹. Determine the speed of the first glider after the collision.
items.markingKey: 2.0 × 6.0 = 2.0v₁ + 1.5 × 4.8 = 2.40 m s⁻¹. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: In which situation is the momentum of the system NOT conserved?
options: A stationary firework explodes in mid-air

A car speeds up because of friction from the road
Two trolleys collide on a frictionless track
items.answer: A car speeds up because of friction from the road
